sources.title: Lynn Margulis (Q234583) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-23): English label 'Lynn Margulis', description 'American evolutionary biologist (1938-2011)', born 5 March 1938, died 22 November 2011, citizenship United States, Korean label '린 마굴리스', English and Korean Wikipedia sitelinks present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Andrew H. Knoll, 'Lynn Margulis, 1938-2011' (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 109(4):1022, January 2012; PubMed Central), read in full: obituary by a Harvard palaeobiologist -- Chicago degree at 18 and Berkeley PhD six years later, two decades at Boston University then Distinguished University Professor at UMass; the 1967 'On the origin of mitosing cells' paper rejected by some 15 journals first, Merezhkovsky's 1905 forerunner, her restating of the idea in cell and molecular terms so it became testable, and the later DNA evidence for chloroplasts and mitochondria (counted by Knoll as one of the great advances of 20th-century science); her claim about the symbiotic origin of flagella never gained strong support; her backing of Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis and an 'alternative biology' of cooperation that put her in lasting conflict with evolutionary biologists; she also questioned HIV's role in AIDS; a 'fountain of ideas' who could infuriate colleagues; her advocacy of science education, especially in less developed countries; her remark that she considered her ideas 'right' not controversial. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Insider obituary in an academy journal, admiring but openly critical in places. Its passages on her maternal manner and family were not used.

EBSCO Research Starters, 'Lynn Margulis' (ebsco.com), read in full: schooling and positions (Chicago, Wisconsin, Berkeley PhD 1965, Brandeis postdoc, Boston University from 1965, UMass Amherst); the 1967 Journal of Theoretical Biology paper rejected by fifteen journals, her renaming of the Merezhkovsky and Kozo-Polyansky idea as endosymbiotic theory; the 1970 book and serial endosymbiosis theory; later data supporting it (organelle DNA resembling bacterial DNA); the claim that flagella and cilia came from spirochetes; her work with Lovelock on Gaia; the 'enormous hostility' her revival of the theory drew, and that she travelled widely to defend it; awards (National Medal of Science, Darwin-Wallace Medal, Guggenheim). Reference overview; the page's reference to 'Lynn Sagan' as author is its own naming inconsistency; its passages on family were not used.

Susan Young, 'Lynn Margulis dead at 73' (Nature news blog, 23 November 2011), read in full: obituary notice with her degrees, UMass professorship, 1983 election to the National Academy of Sciences and 1999 National Medal of Science; endosymbiosis described as initially met with scepticism but now widely accepted; a quotation from UMass dean Steve Goodwin that she believed in 'pushing it to the limits' while conventional scientists tended to 'stop a little too soon' and made connections others wouldn't. Short contemporaneous notice; its family details and cause of death were not used.

Andrew Robinson, 'Earth mother, microbe lover' (Times Higher Education 'Worldly wise' interview profile, 3 July 1998), read in full: her serial endosymbiosis and symbiogenesis claims, five-kingdom classification versus Woese's rival scheme, Gaia as 'symbiosis as seen from space' and her denial of goddess implications; E. O. Wilson calling her 'one of the most successful synthetic thinkers in modern biology'; Richard Dawkins openly hostile and refusing to share a platform, most scientists regarding Gaia as unnecessary or mystical; her paper rejected 15 times and lost by Science; her view that the textbook version of mitochondria is dogmatic; her blunt, combative style in interview. Contemporaneous profile based on an interview, so some content is self-description (not used alone). Its passages on feminism and personal opinions were not used.

Robert Thorson, ''Rebel' Earth Mother Probed Life's Secrets' (University of Connecticut Department of Earth Sciences blog, posted 19 July 2021; column drafted around 2012), read in full: tribute column that summarises endosymbiosis and the rejection of the 1967 paper by more than a dozen journals, her National Academy election (1983), National Medal of Science (1999) and Darwin-Wallace Medal (2008); her Gaia position (rejecting the Earth-as-organism comparison as unscientific); and quotes John Archibald's Current Biology obituary calling her 'amusing, exasperating, enlightening', favouring holistic over reductionist approaches, increasingly dogmatic and criticised and praised in equal measure. The Archibald obituary itself was not opened (quoted at second hand). Popular column, partly admiring and partly critical.

National Center for Science Education, 'Lynn Margulis dies' (ncse.ngo, 23 November 2011), read in full: short notice reporting that endosymbiotic theory beginning with her 1967 paper is now broadly accepted for mitochondria and chloroplasts but not for every organelle she proposed, and that symbiogenesis and Gaia were unconventional mechanisms that antievolutionists have misrepresented; she rejected creationism. Used only to corroborate the partial acceptance of her claims. Advocacy organisation notice; nothing beyond that was used.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'Lynn Margulis.jpg' (with the Commons API record), checked for the portrait's licence: photograph by Javier Pedreira (Wicho), taken 9 November 2005 at a science-communication congress in La Coruna (EXIF date 2005-11-09), self-published by the photographer under CC BY-SA 2.5; 600 x 900 original. Not used for any scoring.

persistence.rationale: [src_margulis_knoll, src_margulis_ebsco, src_margulis_the, src_margulis_thorson, src_margulis_nature | 1967-2011 | academy obituary + reference overview + 1998 profile + tribute column + obituary notice] Knoll, EBSCO, THE and Thorson all report that her 1967 endosymbiosis paper was rejected by some fifteen or more than a dozen journals before publication (THE adds that Science lost it); EBSCO says she kept travelling widely to present and defend the theory in the face of 'enormous hostility'; Nature and Knoll record that the idea was first met with scepticism and later became widely accepted, with the later DNA evidence Knoll describes. A long, dated course of keeping the idea alive through repeated rejection and hostility is reported by five sources, including an independent obituary and a contemporaneous profile, so documented at a moderate-to-good confidence (the rejection count varies between 'a dozen' and fifteen).

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_margulis_knoll, src_margulis_the, src_margulis_thorson, src_margulis_nature, src_margulis_ncse | 1967-2011 | academy obituary + 1998 profile + tribute column quoting a peer obituary + obituary notice + advocacy notice] Knoll says she revived a largely forgotten symbiosis idea and rebuilt it in testable cell and molecular terms, and that endosymbiosis is now counted as one of the great advances of 20th-century science; THE and Thorson (quoting Archibald) describe her as an iconoclast who favoured holistic over reductionist approaches, trusted her own intuition and rejected parts of the textbook account; Knoll adds that her wider claims, including the symbiotic origin of flagella and symbiosis as the driver of speciation, did not win strong support and that she also questioned HIV's role in AIDS; NCSE says her theory is accepted for mitochondria and chloroplasts but not for every organelle she proposed. Holding to an unfashionable view that was later confirmed in its core, and to other views that were not, is described by five sources with both praise and criticism, so documented at a moderate confidence, dual-edged.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_margulis_the, src_margulis_knoll, src_margulis_ebsco, src_margulis_thorson | 1967-2011 | 1998 profile + academy obituary + reference overview + tribute column] THE reports that Richard Dawkins was openly hostile and refused to share a platform with her and that she remained combative in interview; Knoll says her ideas put her in lasting conflict with evolutionary biologists and that she could infuriate colleagues and liked having the last word; EBSCO says her revival of the theory exposed her to enormous hostility and she kept defending it; Thorson, quoting Archibald, calls her criticised and praised in equal measure. Working on in open disagreement with prominent colleagues is described by four sources, but the accounts are of her reputation and manner rather than dated exchanges, and the profile is partly her own voice, so strong inference at a modest confidence, dual-edged because Knoll and Archibald also note the cost in dogmatism.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_margulis_knoll, src_margulis_ebsco, src_margulis_nature, src_margulis_the | 1967-1981 | academy obituary + reference overview + obituary notice + 1998 profile] Knoll notes that Merezhkovsky had proposed a similar idea in 1905 and that Margulis restated it in cell and molecular terms, which made it testable; EBSCO says she revived and renamed the Merezhkovsky and Kozo-Polyansky idea and extended it in books in 1970 and 1981; the UMass dean quoted by Nature says she made connections others would not normally make; E. O. Wilson, quoted by THE, calls her a leading synthetic thinker. The originality lies largely in reviving and rebuilding an earlier proposal, with praise partly retrospective or from admirers, so strong inference at a moderate confidence.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_margulis_knoll, src_margulis_the, src_margulis_ebsco, src_margulis_thorson | 1970-2011 | academy obituary + 1998 profile + reference overview + tribute column] She linked cell biology and microbial evolution to Gaia and Earth-system ideas (Knoll: an alternative biology built on cooperation; THE: Gaia as 'symbiosis as seen from space'; EBSCO: collaboration with Lovelock), moved between botany, biology and geosciences departments at UMass, and proposed a five-kingdom classification of life (THE). A genuine range across cell biology, microbiology and Earth-system thinking is described by four sources, but the Gaia link is mostly her own framing in an interview and Gaia itself was seen by most scientists as unnecessary or mystical (THE), so strong inference at a modest confidence.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_margulis_knoll, src_margulis_thorson, src_margulis_the | 1998-2011 | academy obituary + tribute column quoting a peer obituary + 1998 profile] Knoll reports that her claim for a symbiotic origin of flagella never gained strong support and that she said in her last interview that she did not consider her ideas controversial but right; Thorson, quoting Archibald, calls her increasingly dogmatic; THE records her view that the textbook mitochondria account was dogmatic. Maintaining specific proposals after the field had not supported them is described by three sources, but the sources do not document a specific episode of refusing a particular piece of evidence, and the same trait helped sustain the endosymbiosis claim that was later confirmed, so strong inference at a low-to-modest confidence, dual-edged.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_margulis_knoll, src_margulis_the | 1998-2011 | academy obituary + 1998 profile] Knoll says she championed science education, especially in less developed countries, was fluent in Spanish and was revered by students in Spain and Latin America, and was an evangelist for the importance of bacteria to the biosphere; THE says she prefers doing science to being a public figure. A sustained outreach commitment is described by one detailed obituary with support from the profile, but no specific programmes or dated activities are given, so strong inference at a low-to-modest confidence.
